RESULT: A TWO-TETHER BRIDGE NO-PIN LEMMA
Status: Complete elementary lemma, with a conditional application
to centrally symmetric positive-contact cores.
The full Erdos Problem #99 remains open.

1. Statement

Let P be a finite planar unit-separated configuration of
diameter D, and let C be a subset of its vertices.

Write F for the FULL graph of unit-distance contacts and H
for the FULL graph of diameter-D pairs.

Assume:

(A) Every endpoint of every edge of H belongs to C.

(B) For each connected component B of the induced graph
    F[P\C], one of the following holds:

    (i) B has at most one unit-contact edge to C;

    (ii) B has exactly two unit-contact edges to C,
         and their endpoints within B coincide;

    (iii) B has exactly two unit-contact edges to C,
          with distinct endpoints x,y in B, and some
          bridge of F[B] separates x from y.

Here a bridge is an edge whose deletion disconnects B.

THEOREM.
If P is an ordinary local minimum of diameter subject to
all pairwise distances being at least 1, then the restricted
configuration P|C is itself an ordinary local minimum.

This theorem requires no symmetry, stress, genericity,
planarity of the contact graph, or triangle-free assumption.

In particular, condition (B) holds whenever every external
contact component is a tree with at most two attachments
to C. It also permits arbitrarily large cyclic external
components attached by one tether, and two-tether cyclic
components whose tether sites are separated by a bridge.

The theorem concerns the original FULL contact graph, not
just the positive support of a selected stress.

2. Elementary two-strut translation lemma

Let u_1,u_2 be unit vectors in R^2. Suppose

    u_i(e) = u_i + O(e),  i=1,2,

as e tends to zero through positive values.

Then there exists t(e)=O(sqrt(e)) such that

    |u_1(e)+t(e)| >= 1,
    |u_2(e)+t(e)| >= 1.

Proof.

If u_1+u_2 is nonzero, choose the unit vector

    w = (u_1+u_2)/|u_1+u_2|.

Both scalar products u_i.w are strictly positive.
Taking t(e)=sqrt(e)w gives

    |u_i(e)+t(e)|^2
       = 1+2sqrt(e)(u_i.w)+O(e)>1

for sufficiently small e.

Otherwise u_2=-u_1. Choose a unit vector w perpendicular
to u_1 and put

    t(e)=K sqrt(e)w.

For some constant M, independent of sufficiently small e,

    |u_i(e)+t(e)|^2
       >= 1+(K^2-M)e-O(K e^(3/2)).

Choosing K sufficiently large makes both expressions
strictly greater than 1.

This proves the lemma.

Notice that the two unit vectors can represent contact
edges incident to different moving vertices. Only the
common translation of their endpoints matters.

3. Proof of the theorem

Suppose, toward contradiction, that P|C is not an ordinary
local minimum.

By (A), its original diameter is D. Hence there are
unit-separated configurations Q_j of the labelled vertices
of C such that

    Q_j -> P|C,
    diam(Q_j)<D.

Let e_j be the maximum displacement of a C vertex.
Then e_j -> 0.

We extend each Q_j to all original labels.

Consider one connected component B of F[P\C].

Case (i): No tether.

Keep every vertex of B fixed.

If there is exactly one tether, say ax with a in C and
x in B, translate every vertex of B by

    q_a-p_a.

The tether stays exactly unit length, as do all contacts
internal to B.

Case (ii): Two tethers with the same external endpoint.

Write them ax and bx, allowing a=b only if the two
edges are actually distinct, which is impossible in a
simple contact graph.

After moving a and b to q_a and q_b, choose a common
translation t_j of B using the two-strut lemma, applied
to the original contact vectors

    p_x-p_a,  p_x-p_b.

Both tether lengths remain at least 1. All internal
contact lengths are unchanged.

The translation satisfies t_j -> 0.

Case (iii): Two tethers at distinct external endpoints.

Write the tether edges as ax and by.

Choose a bridge uv of F[B] whose deletion separates x
and y. Let B_x and B_y be the corresponding vertex sets,
with x in B_x and y in B_y.

First translate all of B by q_a-p_a. This preserves its
internal contacts and the tether ax exactly.

Next translate only B_y by an additional vector t_j.

Precisely two previously unit-length constraints can
change under this additional translation:

    the bridge uv;
    the tether by.

Indeed, uv is the only internal contact crossing the
cut because it is a bridge, and by is the only tether
incident to B_y.

Orient the two contact vectors so that their moved
endpoints lie in B_y. Before the additional translation,
both vectors differ by O(e_j) from their original unit
vectors.

Apply the two-strut lemma. It produces

    t_j = O(sqrt(e_j))

making both lengths at least 1.

All other internal contacts and the first tether retain
their lengths.

Thus every component B can be placed so that all
originally active unit constraints are satisfied, and
every external vertex moves by o(1).

Perform these constructions independently for the
finitely many external components.

All FULL F contacts are now feasible.

Every pair outside F had original distance strictly
greater than 1. Finiteness provides a positive minimum
slack over these pairs. Since the entire extended
configuration converges to P, all these inequalities
remain satisfied for sufficiently large j.

Next consider the diameter constraints.

By (A), every pair having at least one endpoint outside
C had original distance strictly less than D. Again,
finiteness provides a positive minimum slack.

Our extensions converge to P, so all these distances
remain strictly below D.

Pairs entirely inside C have distances strictly below D
because diam(Q_j)<D.

Consequently the resulting complete n-point configuration
is unit-separated, converges to P, and has diameter
strictly smaller than D.

This contradicts ordinary local minimality of P.

Therefore P|C is an ordinary local minimum. QED.

4. Application to the original joint-MAX support

Let P be triangle-free, and let (mu,lambda) be an
ORIGINAL joint-MAX physical stress.

Set

    C = V(T),

where T is its positive unit-contact support.

Suppose:

    (1) C is geometrically centrally symmetric;
    (2) every FULL actual diameter endpoint lies in C;
    (3) the FULL zero-positive-contact attachments
        satisfy the two-tether bridge condition above.

The theorem proves that P|C is a centrally symmetric,
triangle-free, ordinary local minimum of diameter D.

Now invoke the separately supplied central classification:

    Every centrally symmetric triangle-free ordinary
    local minimum having at least two vertices is
    either a unit segment or a unit square.

Under that classification, P|C has diameter respectively
1 or sqrt(2). Therefore

    D <= sqrt(2).

Thus no configuration satisfying (1)-(3) can have
D>sqrt(2).

This extends the previously supplied result for an
ORIGINAL FULL contact component containing all actual
diameter endpoints: C need not be a component of F.
There may be genuine zero-weight contact attachments,
including arbitrarily large trees and cyclic blocks.

IMPORTANT DEPENDENCY:
The attachment-transfer theorem above is proved here
without invoking the central classification.

The final D<=sqrt(2) exclusion uses that classification
as an additional theorem supplied in the research notes.
I have not independently reproduced its complete proof
here, and it should not be attributed to Das (2026).

5. Why the two-tether threshold is meaningful

A three-tether attachment can be geometrically trapped,
even without a unit equilateral triangle.

Take one external point x=0 and three fixed anchors

    a_k=(cos(2*pi*k/3),sin(2*pi*k/3)),
    k=0,1,2.

All three edges xa_k have length 1. The mutual distances
between anchors are sqrt(3), so this four-point contact
pattern is triangle-free.

For every nonzero displacement z with |z|<1, at least
one anchor satisfies

    z.a_k >= |z|/2.

Consequently

    |z-a_k|^2
       =1+|z|^2-2z.a_k
       <=1+|z|^2-|z|<1.

Thus x is locally immobilized when its three anchors
are fixed.

This is an exact obstruction to extending the elementary
translation-release argument to arbitrary three-tether
attachments.

It is NOT an example of a full ordinary local minimum,
nor of a centrally symmetric stressed core. It establishes
only that three tethers can create a genuine local cage
which two tethers cannot create by translations.

6. Boundary left unresolved

The theorem does not exclude centrally symmetric
positive-contact cores when:

(a) a zero-weight actual diameter pair has an endpoint
    outside C;

(b) an external component has three or more contacts
    to C;

(c) two distinct tether sites belong to the same
    bridgeless external contact block.

Case (a) is especially important. Positive diameter
support G lying inside C does NOT establish (A).
Joint-MAX does not turn every active H multiplier positive.

Nor does the previously supplied weak-row release theorem
automatically eliminate these additional diameter pairs
while preserving all original positive-core vectors.

Accordingly, the theorem is a genuine restricted
attachment no-go, not a proof that every central
joint-MAX positive core is impossible.

It also does not require or imply that local minima are
global minima.

Related stress and rigidity framework:

Research repository context:

The repository material consulted includes an explicitly
unreviewed population-reserve reconstruction. None of its
numerical estimates or unreviewed claims is used in this
proof.

The two-strut lemma, bridge-extension argument, and
conditional application are elementary deductions presented
here. No historical novelty or publication priority is
claimed.

VERDICT:
A centrally symmetric ORIGINAL positive-contact core cannot
be protected from diameter improvement by zero-weight
external contact components attached through at most two
tethers with the stated bridge structure, provided ALL
actual diameter endpoints already belong to that core.

The remaining boundary is genuine multi-anchor or
zero-weight-diameter pinning, not ordinary pendant-tree
pinning.

1. Theorem (sharp finite periodic strip capacity)

Put a = sqrt(3)/2. Fix H >= 0.

Let P be a locally finite, unit-separated subset of
R x [0,H], invariant under translation by (1,0), containing
the entire fixed boundary row

    Z = {(m,0): m in Z}.

Let N(P) be the number of translation orbits, equivalently
the number of points in [0,1) x [0,H].

No assumption is made that the points form rows. All orbit
heights and horizontal phases are arbitrary.

Write M(H) for the maximum N(P), and M_TF(H) for the
maximum among packings whose FULL unit-distance graph
contains no triangle.

Then

    M(H) = floor(H/a) + 1.

Moreover,

    M_TF(0) = 1,

and for H > 0,

    M_TF(H) = ceil(H/a).

Consequently, for positive H:

    M(H) - M_TF(H)
       = 1  if H/a is an integer,
       = 0  otherwise.

Thus the exact triangle-free correction in this periodic
class is zero at every nonresonant strip height. There is
no positive uniform boundary penalty.

2. Proof of the upper bounds

Choose one representative from each translation orbit,
and order the representatives by height:

    0 = y_0 < y_1 < ... < y_(N-1) <= H.

The first representative is the fixed boundary orbit.

For two distinct orbits represented by (x_i,y_i) and
(x_j,y_j), choose an integer m such that

    |x_i - x_j + m| <= 1/2.

The corresponding translated points are distinct.
Unit separation therefore gives

    1 <= (x_i - x_j + m)^2 + (y_i-y_j)^2
      <= 1/4 + (y_i-y_j)^2.

Hence

    |y_i-y_j| >= sqrt(3)/2 = a.

In particular, orbit heights are distinct, so their
ordering is legitimate, and

    H >= y_(N-1) >= (N-1)a.

Therefore

    N <= floor(H/a) + 1.

This proves the unrestricted upper bound.

Now suppose H = Ja with integer J >= 1, and suppose
a triangle-free packing attained N = J+1.

Equality throughout the height estimate forces

    y_j = ja,   j=0,...,J.

In particular, the first orbit above the boundary has
height exactly a.

For its representative (x,a), unit separation from all
boundary points requires

    (x-m)^2 + a^2 >= 1

for every integer m.

Since a^2 = 3/4, its distance from every integer must
be at least 1/2. But every real number is within 1/2
of some integer. Thus

    x = m + 1/2

for some integer m.

The three points

    (m,0), (m+1,0), (m+1/2,a)

have all three pairwise distances exactly one.

This is a unit equilateral triangle, contradicting TF.

Therefore at resonant positive heights H = Ja,

    N <= J.

At nonresonant heights, the unrestricted bound already
gives

    N <= ceil(H/a).

Combining the cases proves the claimed TF upper bound.

3. Sharpness and all-cross-pair verification

For any h > a and positive integer J, define

    P(J,h) =
      {(m+j/2, jh):
        m in Z, j=0,1,...,J}.

Here j/2 is an actual coordinate, not just a residue.

The boundary row j=0 is exactly Z.

We verify ALL pairs.

Case A: Same row.

For two distinct points their horizontal displacement is
a nonzero integer, so their distance is at least one.
The only unit contacts in a row are consecutive points.

Case B: Adjacent rows.

Their horizontal displacement is a half-integer.
Its absolute value is at least 1/2.

Consequently their squared distance is at least

    1/4 + h^2
      > 1/4 + a^2
      = 1.

Thus every adjacent-row pair is strictly separated.

Case C: Rows differing by at least two.

Their vertical displacement is at least 2h, and

    2h > sqrt(3) > 1.

Therefore these pairs are also strictly separated.

It follows that P(J,h) is a genuine unit-separated
packing, not merely a collection satisfying selected
nearest-neighbor inequalities.

Its FULL unit graph consists exclusively of horizontal
unit edges, so it has no unit triangle.

There are exactly J+1 translation orbits.

Now let H>0 be nonresonant and set

    J = floor(H/a).

If J=0, use the boundary row alone.

If J>=1, choose

    a < h <= H/J.

Every claimed bound is therefore sharp.

5. Scope: arbitrary perturbations and periodicity

The upper-bound proof allows arbitrary orbit heights,
horizontal phases, and numbers of orbits. In particular,
it does not presuppose straight interior rows or a
triangular combinatorial pattern.

It does assume horizontal translation period exactly one.
It is NOT a sharp classification of every packing with

Nevertheless, the explicit packings belong to the larger
classes as well. Therefore they already disprove any
universal positive scallop-area point charge that is
claimed for all periodic or arbitrary triangle-free
boundary packings.

The boundary disks forbid CENTER POSITIONS below f(x).
Their union is not a region whose area may automatically
be converted into missing lattice sites. The first
interior row occupies the valleys of that forbidden-center
frontier, and subsequent staggered rows accommodate the
full triangular-lattice site count.

6. What curvature would still have to supply

This result does not classify globally minimum-diameter
packings or rule out an additional obstruction caused by
a curved unit-edge rim.

For a large odd regular rim or a Reinhardt rim, the
boundary direction changes along successive unit edges.
The local turn is typically O(1/D), unlike the exact
zero turning of Z.

A successful boundary-layer argument would need to show
that this turning produces a NONREMOVABLE loss of packing
sites after optimizing all interior row phases, vertical
offsets, and irregular placements.

In particular, it would need to control:

(a) Compatibility of successive inward layers with the
    changing boundary direction;

(b) Integer site counts and phase closure around the
    entire rim, including Reinhardt carrier arcs;

(c) The resulting loss in actual point count, without
    charging excluded area more than once;

(d) The constraints from the FULL diameter graph and
    all n labels, rather than only boundary contacts.

There is an important scaling warning.

A hypothetical additive local correction bounded by
C times the absolute boundary turn per edge totals only
O(1) over a rim of O(D) edges and total turning O(1).

Such a correction alone cannot provide an Omega(D)
population penalty.

A linear penalty would require, for example, a genuinely
nonlocal phase or layer-capacity obstruction, or some
mechanism amplifying curvature over many inward layers.

No such amplification is proved here.

In particular, oddness or a Reinhardt diameter cycle
must not simply be assumed to create a fixed positive

1. FINITE TURN-ANGLE EXCLUSION LEMMA

Let P be a finite unit-separated planar packing. Suppose its convex
hull K is a strictly convex N-gon whose N sides all have length 1,
and all remaining points of P lie strictly inside K.

Write a = sqrt(3)/2. For each hull side e_i, let T_i be its inward
unit-equilateral apex. Let tau_i in (0,pi) be the exterior turning
angle between consecutive sides e_i and e_(i+1).

For 0 < eps <= 1/32, define the shallow interior population

M(eps) = #{q in P\V(K): dist(q,boundary K) <= a+eps}.

Construct a graph J(eps) on the N hull sides, joining consecutive
sides e_i,e_(i+1) whenever

  |cos(tau_i/2)-sqrt(3)sin(tau_i/2)| + 8eps < 1.       (1)

Then the following exact finite inequality holds:

                  M(eps) <= alpha(J(eps)),             (2)

where alpha is the independence number.

This depends explicitly on the entire turn sequence, not just its
sum. It applies to every interior point label; no stress,
minimality, lattice approximation, or asymptotic assumption is used.

Proof.

Choose any shallow interior point q and a nearest point of
boundary K. That nearest point cannot be a hull vertex: every
distance from q to a hull vertex is at least 1, whereas

                   a+eps < 1.

Consequently the nearest point lies in the interior of some unit
side e_i.

Use coordinates in which e_i has endpoints (-1/2,0),(1/2,0),
and q=(x,h), with |x|<=1/2 and h>0.

The unit-separation conditions imply

            (1/2-|x|)^2+h^2 >= 1.

In particular h>=a. Since h<=a+eps, we obtain

 |x| <= 1/2-sqrt(1-h^2) <= 3eps.                       (3)

For the last inequality, differentiate
f(h)=1/2-sqrt(1-h^2). Throughout
[a,a+1/32], its derivative is less than 3, and f(a)=0.

The inward equilateral apex has coordinates T_i=(0,a).
Therefore

                     |q-T_i| < 4eps.                  (4)

Assign q to the side e_i just selected, breaking ties arbitrarily.

Two shallow points assigned to the same side would be at distance
less than 8eps<1. Thus at most one point is assigned per side.

For consecutive sides, their inward equilateral apices satisfy

 |T_(i+1)-T_i|
       = |cos(tau_i/2)-sqrt(3)sin(tau_i/2)|.           (5)

Indeed, if u,v are the consecutive unit tangent vectors, then
T_(i+1)-T_i=(u+v)/2+a J(v-u), where J denotes counterclockwise
rotation by 90 degrees. Resolving along their angular bisector
gives (5).

If two shallow points were assigned to adjacent sides joined
in J(eps), (4), (5), and the triangle inequality would give

 |q_(i+1)-q_i|
   < 8eps+|cos(tau_i/2)-sqrt(3)sin(tau_i/2)|
   < 1,

contradicting unit separation.

The assigned sides form an independent set in J(eps).
This proves (2).

Take odd N>=25, and set

 R=1/(2sin(phi)),
 D=1/(2sin(phi/2)).

The regular N-gon of circumradius R has unit sides and diameter D.

Its actual diameter graph H joins vertices whose indices differ

single cycle, and every rim vertex is diametrically loaded.

This is the regular odd Reinhardt construction, with Reuleaux

All its exterior turns equal 2phi. Put

Consequently

The bound is sharp, even with a quadratic-size interior population.

Select the alternating rim sides

There are (N-1)/2 selected sides.

For each selected side place an interior point q_i at its inward
equilateral apex, displaced a further eps inward. All these
points lie on a circle of radius

Each q_i has distance

from its two nearest rim vertices. All other rim vertices are

Since N>=25 gives phi<1/7 and a+eps<1,

  2r sin(2phi)

Thus the (N-1)/2 shallow points are mutually strictly separated

Every bulk point is more than distance 1 from every shallow

for every i, with indices modulo N.

distance strictly greater than 1. Thus the FULL unit
graph F is exactly the boundary cycle C_N.

Suppose P is an ordinary local minimum of diameter
among ALL labelled N-point unit-separated planar
configurations, not merely a stationary point among
equilateral polygons.

Let D>1 be its diameter and H its FULL actual
diameter graph.

For EVERY normalized nonnegative physical stress
(mu,lambda) satisfying

    L_F(mu) P = L_H(lambda) P,
    sum_H lambda = 1,

the following hold:

(a) Every boundary-edge multiplier is positive:

    mu_{i,i+1} > 0   for all i.

(b) Every vertex has positive diameter loading:

    sum_{j:ij in H} lambda_ij > 0   for all i.

Consequently, there is an epsilon(P)>0 such that
all quantities in (a) and (b) are at least epsilon(P)
simultaneously for every physical stress.

In particular, H covers all N vertices and

    |E(H)| >= ceil(N/2) = (N+1)/2.

If H is a forest and equality holds, then H consists
of one three-vertex path and (N-3)/2 isolated edges.
In that equality case every actual diameter edge has
positive lambda in every physical stress.

First establish existence of normalized physical stress.

Use the epigraph formulation minimizing t subject to

    |p_i-p_j|^2 >= 1,
    |p_i-p_j|^2 <= t

for every distinct pair.

At (P,D^2), take perturbation velocities v_i=p_i
and epigraph velocity tau=2D^2+1.

Every active unit-distance lower constraint has
directional derivative 2>0.

Every active diameter upper constraint, written as

    t-|p_i-p_j|^2 >= 0,

has directional derivative

    tau-2D^2 = 1>0.

Thus the Mangasarian-Fromovitz constraint
qualification holds. Ordinary local minimality
gives nonnegative KKT multipliers supported on
the FULL active graphs F and H, with

    sum_H lambda = 1
    L_F(mu)P = L_H(lambda)P.

Taking the inner product with P gives

    sum_F mu = D^2.

Hence at least one boundary edge has positive mu.

We now prove that the positive contact support must
contain the entire boundary cycle.

Suppose otherwise. Since the only unit edges are the
boundary edges, the nonempty positive contact support
is a proper subgraph of C_N.

It therefore has a path component with a vertex i
incident to exactly one positive contact edge,
say e=(i,i+1).

Consider the supporting line through p_i,p_{i+1}.
Choose its unit normal u pointing into the polygon.

Strict convexity implies

    u.(p_j-p_i)>0

for every j other than i and i+1.

At vertex i, physical equilibrium is

    mu_e(p_i-p_{i+1})

Take the inner product with u.

The left side is zero because e lies on the
supporting line.

Every term on the right is nonpositive, and any
term having positive lambda is strictly negative:
the pair (i,i+1) cannot be a diameter because
D>1.

Therefore all diameter multipliers incident to i
must vanish.

But the vector equilibrium then reads

    mu_e(p_i-p_{i+1})=0,

contradicting mu_e>0.

Thus no proper nonempty subgraph of the boundary
cycle can support physical contact stress.

It follows that

    mu_{i,i+1}>0

for every boundary edge, proving (a).

Next fix any vertex i. Again take the inward normal u
to the supporting line through p_i,p_{i+1}.

The equilibrium equation at i is now

    mu_{i-1,i}(p_i-p_{i-1})
      + mu_{i,i+1}(p_i-p_{i+1})
       = sum_{j:ij in H} lambda_ij(p_i-p_j).

Its left side has strictly negative inner product
with u: the second term has zero product, while
the first has strictly negative product and
mu_{i-1,i}>0.

Consequently the right side is nonzero, so at least
one diameter multiplier incident to i is positive.

This proves (b).

For the uniform assertion, the physical stress set is
closed. It is bounded because

    0 <= lambda_ij <= 1,
    0 <= mu_ij <= D^2.

It is nonempty by KKT and therefore compact.

Every one of the finitely many continuous quantities
in (a) and (b) is strictly positive throughout this
compact set. Their joint minimum is positive.

Finally, every positive diameter edge loads at most
two vertices, giving

    |E(H)| >= ceil(N/2).

If H is a forest with exactly (N+1)/2 edges and
no isolated vertices, its number of components is

    N-(N+1)/2 = (N-1)/2.

Every component has at least two vertices. Exactly
one component must have three vertices, and all
others two. This gives the asserted forest structure.

Moreover, removing any one diameter edge would
leave fewer than ceil(N/2) positive edges, making
positive loading of every vertex impossible.
Therefore every actual diameter multiplier is positive
in the equality case.

This lemma strengthens the elementary diameter-loading
necessity in the restricted rim-only setting: not only
is every vertex on an actual diameter, but every
physical stress positively loads every vertex and
every unit boundary edge.

The result applies to odd N, but its proof also works
for even N >= 4.

It excludes sparse diameter forests and eliminates
partial positive contact support for rim-only
ordinary local minima.

It does NOT exclude positively loaded diameter forests
with more than ceil(N/2) edges. It does NOT establish
Reinhardt's perimeter equality from first-order

The additional hypothesis F=C_N is essential to this
proof. Extra nonboundary unit contacts invalidate the
path-endpoint argument.

Neither ordinary local minimality nor positive stress
may be inferred from stationarity under restricted
turning-angle variations.

Thus the remaining target, even in the pure-rim
subclass, is to exclude non-Reinhardt positively
loaded diameter forests using genuinely additional
geometric or second-order information.

No extension to general cyclic packing cores, no
same-n global competitor, and no resolution of the
full Erdos Problem #99 is claimed.

1. GENERAL FINITE-DISPLACEMENT IDENTITY

Lemma 1 (stress-energy budget).

Let P=(p_1,...,p_n) be any unit-separated packing of
diameter D admitting a physical stress (mu,lambda), with

  L_F(mu) P = L_H(lambda) P,
  sum_F mu = D^2,
  sum_H lambda = 1.

Set Omega=L_F(mu)-L_H(lambda).

For ANY other unit-separated configuration Q on the same
n labels, with actual diameter D' <= D, put U=Q-P. Then

  D^2-(D')^2 <= tr(U^T Omega U).                 (1)

Moreover, for every twice-differentiable path Q(t) with
Q(0)=P and velocity V=Q'(0),

  d^2/dt^2 [tr(Q(t)^T Omega Q(t))] at t=0
       = 2 tr(V^T Omega V).                     (2)

The acceleration Q''(0) cancels exactly.

Proof.

Since every positive contact has squared length 1 and
every positive diameter pair has squared length D^2,

  tr(P^T Omega P)
    = sum_F mu - D^2 sum_H lambda
    = 0.

Stationarity gives Omega P=0. Thus, for Q=P+U,

  tr(Q^T Omega Q)=tr(U^T Omega U).              (3)

Because Q is unit-separated,

  sum_F mu_ij |q_i-q_j|^2 >= sum_F mu_ij=D^2.

Because its FULL actual diameter is D',

  sum_H lambda_ij |q_i-q_j|^2 <= (D')^2.

Subtracting proves (1). Expanding (3) along a path
proves (2), without requiring that path to be feasible.

This argument does not require the supplied universal

constraints: a genuinely feasible Q must satisfy every

pairs, each of length D.

Every such Q satisfies

RESULT: TWO-ANCHOR TREE TRANSPARENCY LEMMA

Status: Rigorous finite-extension lemma, with a sharp three-anchor
kinematic obstruction. It does not resolve Erdos Problem #99.
No mixed-rank assumption, PSD theorem, or unproved vector-preserving
release is used.

1. Statement

Let P be a finite planar packing with all pairwise distances at
least 1 and diameter D. Partition its labels into a core C and a
nonempty exterior set U.

Assume:

(A) No vertex of U is an endpoint of an actual D-edge.

(B) Every unit edge having an endpoint in U belongs to a specified
    connected graph K on U together with at most two distinct
    anchor vertices A,B in C.

(C) K is a tree, and each anchor is a leaf of K.

No restriction is imposed on unit contacts within C.

Let Q_C(t), 0 <= t <= epsilon, be any prescribed continuous motion
of the core satisfying

    Q_c(0) = P_c,
    |Q_c(t)-P_c| <= M*t

for some finite M, with all core-core distances remaining in
[1,D].

THEOREM.

There exists epsilon' > 0 and a continuous extension Q_U(t),
defined for 0 <= t <= epsilon', such that

(i)  Q_u(0) = P_u for every u in U;

(ii) every unit edge of K has length STRICTLY GREATER than 1
     for every sufficiently small t > 0;

(iii) all pairwise distances in the completed packing remain
      between 1 and D.

Consequently, such an exterior tree cannot prevent any prescribed
Lipschitz central-even finite opening motion of C.

The conclusion remains valid for finitely many disjoint exterior
trees satisfying these hypotheses, provided there are no unit
contacts between distinct trees.

Importantly, the theorem does not assume that contact multipliers
on K vanish. It therefore applies in particular when every joint
MAX physical stress assigns zero weight to K.


2. Proof: nonstraight anchored paths

Give every edge e={i,j} of K the linear expression

    a_e(z) = (P_i-P_j) dot (z_i-z_j),

where z is variable on U and zero on all anchors.

We first claim:

Unless K has two anchors joined by a straight, monotone chain
of unit edges, there exists z with

    a_e(z) > 0

simultaneously for every edge e of K.

To prove this, apply the finite-dimensional strict alternative:
either such z exists, or there is a nonzero family tau_e >= 0
satisfying

    sum_{e incident to u} tau_e(P_u-P_other(e)) = 0

at every exterior vertex u.

This alternative follows directly by separating the image of
the linear map z -> (a_e(z)) from the open positive orthant.

Suppose the second alternative holds.

At an exterior leaf, force equilibrium forces its incident
weight to vanish. Repeatedly delete such zero-weight branches.

With zero or one anchor, this eliminates every edge, a
contradiction.

With two anchors, all positive-weight edges must lie on the
unique path joining the anchors. At every interior vertex of
that path, equilibrium involves at most two positive edges.

Two nonzero vectors can balance with nonnegative coefficients
only if they point in exactly opposite directions.

Because every edge has length 1, successive path edges must
therefore have the same direction and equal positive weight.

Thus a nonzero tau exists only when the entire anchor-to-anchor
path is a straight monotone chain.

This proves the claim.

Now choose z with all a_e(z)>0.

Because Q_C(t)-P_C=O(t), set

    Q_u(t) = P_u + L*t*z_u

for exterior vertices, where L is a sufficiently large fixed
positive constant.

For every edge e of K, its squared length becomes

    1 + 2*L*t*a_e(z) + O(t) + O(t^2),

where the first O(t) term comes from prescribed anchor motion
and has a bound independent of L.

Choosing L sufficiently large makes every edge strictly longer
than 1 for all sufficiently small t>0.

All originally inactive distances remain strictly feasible by
continuity and finiteness. Since U has no actual diameter
endpoint, all distances involving U remain below D.

This proves the nonstraight case.


3. Proof: the exceptional straight chain

Let the two anchors be A,B and suppose their path in K is

    p_0=A, p_1, ..., p_L=B,

with L>=2 and

    p_j = p_0 + j*e,   |e|=1.

(The endpoints are anchor leaves, and U is nonempty.)

Choose a fixed unit vector n perpendicular to e.

Put

    s_0=s_L=0,
    s_j=(-1)^j for 1<=j<=L-1.

Every difference s_{j+1}-s_j is nonzero.

For a constant H>0 to be chosen, define the path motion

    q_j(t) =
       Q_A(t) + (j/L)*(Q_B(t)-Q_A(t))
       + H*sqrt(t)*s_j*n.

The endpoints agree exactly with the prescribed anchor motion.

Writing

    e(t)=(Q_B(t)-Q_A(t))/L = e+O(t),

the squared length of consecutive path edges is

    |e(t)+H*sqrt(t)*(s_{j+1}-s_j)*n|^2
      = 1 + H^2*t*(s_{j+1}-s_j)^2
            + O(t) + O(H*t^(3/2)).

The O(t) bound independent of H follows from the assumed
O(t) movement of both anchors.

Choose H sufficiently large. Then every path edge is strictly
longer than 1 for sufficiently small positive t.

Each component branching off this path attaches at exactly
one path vertex p_j, because K is a tree.

For every vertex w in such a branch define

    Q_w(t) = q_j(t) + (1+t)*(P_w-p_j).

Every branch edge, including its attachment edge, is stretched
by the factor 1+t.

Thus every edge of K opens strictly.

Again, inactive inequalities remain valid by continuity.
No exterior D-edge exists, so the completed configuration has
diameter at most D.

This completes the proof.

Notice that the square-root displacement is essential to this
construction. A first-order obstruction need not be a finite
obstruction.

For example, put

    A=(-1,0), B=(1,0), X=(0,0).

If the anchors approach at first order, no velocity of X can
increase both unit distances at first order. Nevertheless,

    A(t)=(-1+t,0),
    B(t)=(1-t,0),
    X(t)=(0,H*sqrt(t))

gives both squared contact lengths

    (1-t)^2+H^2*t > 1

for small t>0 whenever H^2>2.


4. Why three anchors are genuinely different

Consider the three fixed anchor directions

    a_j=(cos(2*pi*j/3),sin(2*pi*j/3)),
    j=0,1,2,

and the exterior vertex X=(0,0).

All three spokes have unit length. Anchor-anchor distances

RESULT: PROVED -- convex triangle-free unit-rhombus tilings
admit no ordinary local diameter minimum except the unit square.

This proof is elementary and does not use the supplied central
classification, positive stresses, PSD, or global optimality.
In particular, no unproved extension of train-track offsets is used.

THEOREM

Let P be a finite unit-separated planar point set with at least
one nondegenerate tile. Suppose:

(1) Its full unit-distance graph contains no triangle.
(2) Its convex hull K is tiled, without overlapping interiors,
    by nondegenerate rhombi of side length 1.
(3) Every tile vertex belongs to P, and every point of P is a
    tile vertex.

If P is an ordinary local minimum of diameter among all
unit-separated sets with |P| labelled points, then P consists
of the four vertices of a unit square.

Conversely, the unit square is a global diameter minimum
among four-point unit-separated sets.

PROOF

Step 1. The tiling is edge-to-edge.

A vertex of one tile cannot lie strictly inside an edge of
another tile: that edge has length 1, so the additional vertex
would be at distance strictly less than 1 from an endpoint.

Likewise, two distinct unit tile edges cannot partially
overlap without sharing both endpoints.

Consequently the rhombi form an ordinary finite edge-to-edge
cell decomposition of the convex polygon K.

Step 2. Every pair of distinct tile-edge axes occurs together
in a rhombus.

Here an axis means an unoriented direction, modulo 180 degrees.

Fix an axis u occurring among tile edges, and choose a unit
normal n_u to u.

In each rhombus having edges parallel to u, join the midpoints
of those opposite edges by a straight segment.

Across shared u-edges these segments concatenate into tracks.
Orient each segment toward increasing scalar projection on n_u.

This orientation is consistent across tiles. Indeed, the two
tiles incident to an interior u-edge lie on opposite sides of
its supporting line. The incoming tile is below that edge in
the n_u coordinate, and the outgoing tile is above it.

Thus every track is strictly increasing in its n_u coordinate.

It follows that:

(a) No track is closed or self-intersecting.
(b) Every track has two endpoints on boundary u-edges.
(c) Its endpoints lie on opposite supporting sides of K.

For (c), use convexity: every boundary edge parallel to u
lies on a supporting line perpendicular to n_u, hence at
either the minimum or maximum n_u projection of K.
Strict increase excludes endpoints on the same side.

In particular, K has two opposite boundary sides parallel
to u, and each u-track joins them.

Now fix any different tile-edge axis v.

The same argument gives tracks joining the two opposite
boundary sides parallel to v.

Because K is convex, the four sides belonging to axes u
and v occur in alternating cyclic order around its boundary.
This follows directly from the cyclic monotonicity of the
oriented tangent direction of a convex polygon: its boundary
directions occur in the order u, v, -u, -v, or the reverse
order, up to cyclic rotation.

Take any u-track and any v-track.

Their endpoints alternate around the boundary of the disk K.
Two embedded arcs in a disk whose endpoints alternate must
intersect. This is the elementary Jordan-arc separation
property.

Tracks meet only in tile interiors, since they meet tile
edges at midpoints and axes u and v have different edge
directions.

Inside a tile, a track crosses between opposite edges.
Therefore an intersection of a u-track and a v-track occurs
in a rhombus having edges parallel to both u and v.

Hence:

(*) Every pair of distinct tile-edge axes occurs together
    in at least one rhombus.

Notice that (*) is stronger than merely asserting the
existence of global train-track offsets. No such offsets
have been assumed.

Step 3. There are exactly two axes.

In a unit rhombus, let alpha be its smaller interior angle.

Unit separation requires alpha >= 60 degrees. Otherwise its
shorter diagonal would have length

    2 sin(alpha/2) < 1.

Equality alpha = 60 degrees would make three tile vertices
a unit equilateral triangle, contrary to assumption (1).

Therefore every tile has

    60 degrees < alpha <= 90 degrees.

By (*), the smaller angle between any two distinct tile-edge
axes exceeds 60 degrees.

But the space of unoriented directions is a circle of
circumference 180 degrees.

If three distinct axes had pairwise smaller angular distances
greater than 60 degrees, their three successive cyclic gaps
would all exceed 60 degrees, contradicting the fact that
their sum is 180 degrees.

Thus there are at most two axes.

Every nondegenerate rhombus uses two distinct axes, so there
are exactly two.

Call their unit direction vectors u and v. Choose their
orientations so that their mutual angle theta satisfies

    60 degrees < theta < 120 degrees.

Step 4. The entire tiling is a full M-by-N rhombic grid.

Every boundary edge is parallel to u or v.

Since K is a nondegenerate convex polygon, its oriented edge
directions turn monotonically around the boundary. With only
the axes u and v available, K has exactly four geometric
sides (allowing collinear subdivisions).

Thus K is a parallelogram.

Every boundary edge is a unit segment. Hence its adjacent
side lengths are positive integers M and N.

Choose a corner p0 and orientations of u,v along its two
outgoing sides. Then

    K = {p0 + s*u + t*v : 0 <= s <= M, 0 <= t <= N}.

The tiling edge graph is connected. Every tile edge vector
is one of +u, -u, +v, -v.

Therefore every tile vertex has the form

    p0 + i*u + j*v

with integer i,j.

Apply the invertible affine coordinate change

    p0 + s*u + t*v  -->  (s,t).

Under this map K becomes the rectangle [0,M] x [0,N],
and every tile becomes an axis-aligned unit square having
integer vertices.

Because these squares tile the whole rectangle, their
collection is precisely its MN standard unit squares.

Consequently

    P = {p0 + i*u + j*v :
         0 <= i <= M, 0 <= j <= N},

where i,j are integers.

This establishes the global grid structure without assuming
it from the mere existence of opposite faces.

In particular, P is centrally symmetric, but we do not need
the central-classification theorem.

Step 5. A nonorthogonal grid is not locally optimal.

For the grid above, its diameter is

    D^2 = M^2 + N^2 + 2MN*|cos(theta)|.

Indeed, the maximum distance over a parallelogram is
attained by its vertices, and the two diagonal lengths
squared are

    M^2 + N^2 +/- 2MN*cos(theta).

Because 60 < theta < 120 degrees, every pair of distinct
grid points other than adjacent row or column neighbors
has distance strictly greater than 1.

For completeness, if its coordinate difference is (a,b),
then

    distance^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab*cos(theta),

and |cos(theta)| < 1/2.

For nonzero integers a,b, this exceeds 1 when
|a|=|b|=1, and is at least 3 otherwise.
If one coordinate vanishes, every non-neighbor difference
has distance at least 2.

Hence the only unit contacts are the horizontal and vertical
grid edges.

Now continuously rotate v toward perpendicularity to u,
keeping |u|=|v|=1.

Every original unit contact remains exactly 1, and all
other distances remain greater than 1 for sufficiently
small perturbations.

But |cos(theta)| strictly decreases.

Therefore D strictly decreases.

Thus a locally optimal grid must have theta = 90 degrees.

Apply a rigid motion so that

    p(i,j) = (i,j),
    0 <= i <= M, 0 <= j <= N.

For a small nonzero real t, replace its horizontal coordinate
chain by

    A_0(t) = (0,0),
    A_1(t) = (cos(t),sin(t)),
    A_i(t) = (i-2+2*cos(t),0),  2 <= i <= M.

Define the deformed points by

    p_t(i,j) = A_i(t) + (0,j).

Every former horizontal unit edge remains exactly unit:

    |A_1-A_0| = 1,
    |A_2-A_1| = 1,

and all subsequent horizontal steps have length 1.

Every vertical unit edge also remains exactly unit.

All former noncontact pairs have distance strictly greater
than 1 at t=0, so continuity and finiteness preserve unit
separation for sufficiently small |t|.

At t=0, the only diameter pairs are the two opposite-corner
pairs, both having distance

    sqrt(M^2+N^2).

For t nonzero and sufficiently small, both have distance

    sqrt((M-2+2*cos(t))^2+N^2)

Every other pair had a strict diameter gap at t=0.
Finiteness and continuity preserve that strict gap for all
sufficiently small t.

Thus every pair has distance strictly less than the original
diameter.

This is an arbitrarily small feasible strict improvement.

Therefore M >= 2 is impossible at an ordinary local minimum.

Interchanging the two coordinate axes proves that N >= 2
is likewise impossible.

Hence

    M = N = 1.

By Step 5 its angle must be 90 degrees.

This proves the forward implication.

For the converse, consider any four unit-separated points.
